name: Ayutla Mixtec
confidence_why: Pankratz & Pike 1967, the only full phonology of Ayutla Mixtec, place word stress by tone within the couplet and its enclitics (the first high tone before a lower tone, else the first high, else the couplet's first syllable), a description de Lacy 2002 and McKendry 2013 restate in full with the original data; Herrera Zendejas 2014 says only that stress usually falls on the first mora and Hills 1990 puts focus stress on the first syllable, both compatible with that default, and McKendry 2013's worry that the tone-driven shifts were heard rather than measured comes with no counter-data.

catalog_quote: Si bien el acento de la palabra, siguiendo el parecido de familia, suele estar en la primera mora ... (Herrera 2014: 59) ... has a word-stress which occurs on the couplet or on a postcouplet syllable. Word-stress occurs on the first couplet or postcouplet syllable with a tone 1 which is contiguously followed by tone 3. ... (A precouplet syllable never has word-stress even if tone 1. ...) If there is no 13 sequence, word-stress occurs on a syllable with tone 2 of a 23 sequence ... neither the sequence 13, nor 23, word-stress occurs on the first tone 1 of the couplet or postcouplet; if there is no tone 1, then it occurs on the first syllable of the couplet ... Word-stress is predictable by tone provided that the couplet occurs word-initially, but it is not predictable if the couplet occurs elsewhere. Phrase-stress, however, is independent both of tone and of the couplet (10). ... has word-stress on the first syllable, and when prepause it has phrase-stress on the last syllable. (Pankratz & Pike 1967: 293, 295; archive.org highlights, IJAL issue and Brend 1975 reprint; tones 1/2/3 = H/M/L) ... (7) a. Stress the leftmost H-toned syllable immediately followed by a L-toned syllable ... b. Else stress the leftmost H-toned syllable ... c. Else stress the leftmost M-toned syllable immediately followed by a L-toned syllable ... d. Else stress the leftmost syllable ... No secondary stress is reported. (de Lacy 2002: 5-7)
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ayutla Mixtec is a three-tone language (H, M, L; tone contrastive at word level). The minimal word is a bimoraic couplet and word accent normally falls on its first mora, i.e. root-/couplet-initial stress, as in other Mixtec languages (Herrera Zendejas, own field data from Coscatlán). The fuller primary account (Pankratz & Pike 1967, seen only via de Lacy 2002) makes placement tone-conditioned within the root+suffix domain: leftmost H followed by L, else leftmost H, else leftmost M followed by L, else the leftmost syllable; prefixes and proclitics are never stressed; correlates are duration and raised pitch.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Herrera says nothing about secondary stress; de Lacy 2002 (p. 7), summarising Pankratz & Pike 1967: 'No secondary stress is reported.'
new_statements.exceptions: Herrera hedges with 'suele' (usually) and gives no exceptions; she defers phrase-level accent and its acoustic correlates to future work (p. 75). Pankratz & Pike 1967 (via de Lacy) report stress shifting off the initial syllable onto a later H-toned (or M+L) syllable, including onto enclitics/suffixes, e.g. [kaʔ.iʔ 'ra ri] 'he (man) will eat him (animal)' vs ['kaʔ.iʔ] 'to eat'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level: Herrera states the word (bimoraic couplet = minimal word) is the domain of tonal and accentual distinctions; her forms are isolation/citation forms from two speakers of Coscatlán, mun. Ayutla de los Libres. P&P/de Lacy: stress domain = root plus suffixes/enclitics (Prosodic Word), excluding prefixes and proclitics.
new_statements.identity_note: Herrera Zendejas's chapter is explicitly labelled 'Patrones fónicos del mixteco (ISO miy)' and is based on her own recordings of two speakers from Coscatlán, municipio de Ayutla de los Libres, Guerrero (fn. 1, p. 46) — i.e. Ayutla Mixtec, ayut1236. Pankratz & Pike 1967 (seen only second-hand via de Lacy) describe the Ayutla town variety; same glottocode. Not to be confused with Ixtayutla Mixtec (Oaxaca), a different language.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Herrera 2014 statement (stress usually on the first mora): Hills locates (focus) stress on the first syllable of the stressed word and gives its phonetic cues (length + throat stricture). It does not state a general word-stress rule and does not mention the tone-driven displacement claimed by Pankratz & Pike 1967. Weak evidence: one parenthetical sentence in a syntax sketch.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Three-tone language; the one-paragraph phonology section gives no word-stress rule and defers to Pankratz & Pike 1967. The only stress statement is about focus: a focused sentence-initial element is stressed, and that stress is realised as length plus glottal stricture on the FIRST syllable of the stressed word. Third-person pronouns are classed as 'poststressed' (enclitic after the stressed host) vs 'prestressed' (before a following noun-phrase element), i.e. clitics are defined by position relative to the stressed word.
new_statements.exceptions: none stated; the p. 87 remark concerns focus stress only, not a general word-stress rule

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the Herrera 2014 statement (stress 'suele estar en la primera mora'): the default is the initial syllable of the couplet, but it adds the Pankratz & Pike tone-driven displacement (stress attracted to a High or Mid syllable before a lower tone), the domain (root + following suffixes, not prefixes) and the phonetic correlate (duration), plus McKendry's caveat that the placement is impressionistic. The dissertation's own primary data are South-eastern Nochixtlán Mixtec (MXY), for which it reports initial root stress and no tone-stress link; only sec. 3.4.1 and scattered remarks concern Ayutla, and those are taken from Pankratz & Pike 1967.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Second-hand restatement of Pankratz & Pike 1967: word stress is predictable from tone; it goes to a High tone followed by a lower tone or a Mid followed by Low; otherwise (no such tonal drop) it falls on the initial syllable of the disyllabic couplet (root). Stress may fall on High-toned suffixes/enclitics after the couplet (e.g. -ká 'more') but never on pre-couplet prefixes even when High-toned. Stressed syllables reported as longer; unstressed vowels may devoice or delete. McKendry doubts these judgements (no acoustic data; the stress was perceived where an English listener would hear it, p. 62-63) and finds for her own language MXY root-initial stress with no tone-stress relation.
new_statements.exceptions: stress shifts to a High tone before a lower tone or Mid before Low (e.g. láˈʃá 'orange' second syllable); stress on post-couplet High-toned enclitics; no stress on prefixes even with High tone (kàʧíˀ 'cotton' compound); optional devoicing/deletion of unstressed vowels

Herrera 2014 (source of the catalog statement): Coscatlán, mun. Ayutla de los Libres. McKendry 2013: primary data are South-eastern Nochixtlán Mixtec [mxy]; its Ayutla statements are second-hand from Pankratz & Pike 1967. Preface of vol. 2: Ayutla Mixtec = Southern Lowlands group, retains word-final glottal stop.

new_statements.quote: [p. 46] Al igual que otras lenguas otomangues el mixteco es una lengua tonal, es decir, la altura de la tonía es contrastiva a nivel de la palabra. // [p. 57] la palabra es la unidad donde se establecen las distinciones tonales y acentuales. // [p. 59] Si bien el acento de la palabra, siguiendo el parecido de familia, suele estar en la primera mora, los ejemplos anteriores impiden establecer una relación entre el acento y el cierre glotal y con ello alejan la posibilidad de interpretarlo como un rasgo prosódico, ya que habría vocales átonas con cierre glotal y tónicas sin cierre glotal.
new_statements.translation: [46] Like other Otomanguean languages Mixtec is a tone language, i.e. pitch height is contrastive at the word level. [57] the word is the unit in which the tonal and accentual distinctions are established. [59] Although word stress, in keeping with the family resemblance, is usually on the first mora, the preceding examples prevent establishing any relation between stress and the glottal stop and so rule out interpreting it [the glottal stop] as a prosodic feature, since there would be unstressed vowels with a glottal stop and stressed ones without. (p. 74, Conclusión, adds that 'el estudio del acento en la frase fonológica y sus correlatos acústicos' remains to be done.)

new_statements.relation_note: This is the same text the catalog record already quotes as '(Herrera 2014: 59)' and the same as existing statement 1 (verified); the 2009 first edition adds nothing beyond it as far as can be determined, since the 2014 volume is the enlarged edition containing the 2009 Mixtec chapter. Relative to the catalog's primary description (Pankratz & Pike 1967: tone-driven word stress on couplet/postcouplet syllables, default first couplet syllable), Herrera's 'usually on the first mora' matches the default placement and is silent on tone-conditioned placement; no contradiction.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Coscatlán (Ayutla de los Libres) Mixtec is a tone language; the chapter has no stress section (its sections are segmental structures, tone, glottal stop/laryngealized vowels) and treats word stress only in passing: the word (bimoraic minimal word = couplet) is the domain of tonal and accentual distinctions, and word stress 'usually' falls on the first mora, as elsewhere in Mixtec; the contrastive word-final glottal stop is independent of stress; phrase-level stress and its acoustic correlates are explicitly left for future work.
new_statements.exceptions: none enumerated; the placement is hedged with 'suele' (usually); no mention of the tone-conditioned stress shifts that Pankratz & Pike 1967 describe
new_statements.identity_note: Herrera's chapter describes the Mixtec of Coscatlán, municipio de Ayutla de los Libres, Guerrero (two male speakers c. 25 years old; p. 46 + fn. 1), i.e. Glottolog ayut1236 Ayutla Mixtec (ISO miy, the code the 2014 chapter title carries); Pankratz & Pike 1967 and Hills 1990 describe Ayutla Mixtec of the same municipio (Hills: Tepango and Coapinola).

readall_conflicts: A mild disagreement on placement, not on type. Herrera Zendejas 2014 (existing catalog statement, Coscatlán data) says word stress 'suele estar en la primera mora' and finds no relation between stress and glottal closure. Pankratz & Pike 1967, as restated by McKendry 2013 (and by de Lacy 2002 already held by the project), say stress is predictable from tone: default on the initial syllable of the couplet, but attracted to a High before a lower tone or a Mid before Low, and to High-toned post-couplet enclitics, never to prefixes. Herrera's 'suele' (usually) leaves room for the P&P exceptions, so the two are compatible on the default but differ on whether tone displaces stress. McKendry herself distrusts the P&P placement (no acoustic measurements; stress heard where English listeners hear it). Hills 1990 gives no word-stress rule; its focus-stress remark (length plus throat stricture on the first syllable of the stressed word) sides with initial placement.
